P1.evidence: Referenced the prospect's pre-call message — 'first of all, a few things that actually sent to me' and later 'I saw your message. It was quite a message that you sent me' — which is the P1a move. Frame was three-part with an unusual addition ('How I want this call to be seen is basically that I already want to coach you'), missing the 'what you need' element. Agreement taken ('Okay. Sounds good.'). Open question run.

P2.evidence: Age, height and weight taken. Injuries covered in genuine depth — the rep pushed properly on the back pain, established it was constant for 30 years, got the 2/10 rating, the triggers and the spasm episodes. Diet and current activity both covered well. But health conditions and medications were never asked as a category, despite muscle relaxers being volunteered; work was only established incidentally; sleep and energy absent. Critically, having established an active labrum tear under physical therapy, no question was asked about what the treating clinicians permit.

P3.evidence: Genuinely good work. Got past aesthetics quickly when the prospect said he did not care about them, correctly identified longevity as the goal, and then drove into family properly: 'You did mention you want to be a better husband, of course, to your wife, and you also want to be there more for your son. Can you take me a little bit more into those things?' That produced the strongest material on the call — the regret about his sons and 'my wife has been working out for years and years. She puts me to shame.' The rep also coached the language, challenging 'should've' into 'going to do'.

P4.evidence: Full sequence. Traced the $1,400/month trainer, established it lasted four months, established what broke it (a two-and-a-half month trip), and pushed until the prospect named the root cause himself: 'I have found that out about myself. If it requires a lot of thought, it's hard for me to stick to it.' That is a precise gap statement and the rep earned it.

P5.evidence: Not run. No two-year picture, no settling question, no 'why not'. The closest move was early and framed as a hypothetical — 'It is then also the moment for you to actually cut that rope on the pendulum and actually go for it... Otherwise, you're going to be continuing doing the same thing that you're doing.' The prospect had arrived pre-sold and self-convicted, so the rep did not need it — which is exactly the situation where the phase gets skipped and nobody notices.

P6.evidence: The belief question was asked in a weaker form after the pillars — 'Do you feel like that's good? We're to help you get to the goals' → 'Yeah, that sounds ideal.' The all-in question was never asked. P6c is a hit only in the trivial sense that no hesitation surfaced. The prospect was self-committed before the call started ('I've already made the decision. Now I'm just trying to find the how'), so the commitment check was never tested.

P11.evidence: Step 2 done properly and immediately — onboarding with Trevor booked for Monday 2:45pm CT with the invite sent on the call. Step 1 was in progress when the recording ended: link sent, form partly completed, prospect leaving to get his card. Step 3 was never mentioned at all — no agreement email, nothing signed on the call. Step 4 was described in the pillar presentation rather than executed as an onboarding instruction. The call ends mid-transaction, so P11 cannot be scored as complete.

objection_plays.detail: The money question was raised gently — 'I think the only thing is the cost, the financial cost' — and the rep ran the isolation move correctly before answering: 'Outside of that being important, the most important thing is if you actually see this fitting in.' The price was then named and accepted immediately, so no further OC moves were needed or run. Correctly stopped rather than over-playing.

The unscripted issue that dominates this call is clinical fit, and it never became an objection because neither party raised it as one. The prospect volunteered an unrepaired labrum tear under active physical therapy, a re-injury four months prior, and 30 years of lumbar pain with recurrent incapacitating spasms. The playbook has no clearance step, no contraindication list and no referral path, so the rep improvised reassurance — 'we're always going to start with making sure that the form is, especially when you've had an injury before, 150% good' — and moved on. This is the known script gap producing its worst outcome: not a lost deal, a completed one.

notes: Phases 3 and 4 were run properly and the close was clean and unforced, so on pure sales process this is a good call. Two things to correct anyway. Phase 5 was skipped entirely because the prospect was pre-sold — an easy habit to form and a bad one. And the more serious point is not an adherence point at all: a prospect in active physical therapy for a torn labrum was taken through the entire process and closed without a single question about what his physical therapist or surgeon permits. The rep opened by saying 'we need to make sure we don't make it worse' and then had no mechanism to act on it.
